newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: FEATURE-Dissenting economists say EMU for Ireland is a mistake.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Dissenting economists say EMU for Ireland is a mistake.

text.p: Ireland's rush to join European economic and monetary union (EMU) has raised the hackles of dissenting economists who say it is a politically-motivated mistake.
All the major political parties and many analysts in Ireland argue that EMU is the next logical step for a country that EU Commission President Jacques Santer has dubbed "a model EU state."

But, against a background of sharp currency gyrations, an increasing number of economists are saying membership is driven more by historical antagonism for Ireland's former colonial master, Britain, than by sound economic sense.
They say it would be wiser for Ireland, like Britain, to delay its entry into EMU until the ambitious and volatile project has worked out its teething problems.

Economists argue that if EMU works well then countries like Britain will most probably join and Ireland can follow suit. If Britain does not join, it will probably be because the Union has not worked and Ireland should not be in there anyway, they say.

"Ireland's historical antipathy towards Britain, its seeking to come out from under Britain's coat tails, is the main driving force for Ireland's questionable drive into EMU," said Jim O'Leary, chief economist with Davy stockbrokers.

"It reminds me of the peasant whose greatest ambition in life was to change landlord," O'Leary told Reuters. "We had British landlords for 800 years and we want to replace them with European landlords."

There is serious anti-EMU sentiment at the grassroots level in some of the EU's major member states, including Germany and France whose governments were the original twin engines of European integration.

Even the EU's biggest and strongest economies, notably Germany, face trouble in paring their budget deficits to the three percent of gross domestic product required to qualify for EMU at its planned launch in 1999.
This has raised fears that the new common currency will be relatively weak.
As the Irish pound continues to contort with every twist and turn towards EMU, there is growing concern in financial markets about Ireland's fate when trapped within a single currency.

"In 1992-93 we were forced to devalue because of a sharp sterling movement. Now we are getting speculation about a revaluation because of another sharp sterling movement," said Jim Power, a Bank of Ireland Group treasury economist.
WHAT HAPPENS IF STERLING STAYS OUT OF EMU?
Power queries what will happen after January 1, 1999 if there is another sharp sterling movement and Ireland is locked into a single currency regime.
The Irish pound will be trapped without the flexibility to adjust to that sterling movement.

"The political elite was driven, during the 1992-3 currency crisis, by a sense of nationalistic fervour to further sever the relationship with the UK and sterling," said one senior economist who asked not to be named.
"I think that sort of mentality still guides Irish policy to a large extent."
O'Leary said the Irish economy is utterly different in structure, performance, cyclicality and trading patterns from any other of the mainland European economies.

So by joining the single currency, the authorities will be subjecting Ireland to a regime in which interest rates and exchange rates will be determined with reference to economic conditions in the Union as a whole.

"Given what we know about the Irish economy in recent years, it is highly unlikely that the interest rate and exchange rate regime, appropriate to a single currency, will be appropriate to Ireland," O'Leary said.
He said one of the best ways of illustrating the risks of EMU was to look at where Ireland would be if it was already a member of the single currency.

"Obviously we would have an exchange rate against the mark 12 percent lower that it currently is and we would be 12 percent lower against sterling and nobody can convince me that Ireland warrants or is suited to a sterling/Irish regime at around 77 pence stg."
WHAT IF IRELAND STAYED OUT OF EMU's FIRST ROUND?

"I do not think it would do us any damage to stay out in round one (in 1999)," O'Leary said. "One of the perceived risks is that the Irish pound would become known as nothing more than a satellite of sterling."
O'Leary said he had no doubt that with a proper policy outside of EMU, Ireland could pursue an existence outside of sterling and as an independent currency.

"We could incorporate similar criteria to the Maastricht stability and growth requirements into domestic legislation in order to reassure financial markets that if we were staying out of EMU we were still going to adhere to prudent fiscal management," he said.
Bank of Ireland's Power said that even if the pound was linked to sterling there is nothing wrong with that.
"In the 1970s there may have been justification for not being attached to sterling and the British economy as it was perceived to be more unstable," he said.
"But UK economic management has improved quite dramatically in the last decade and has become a low inflation and reasonably well-managed economy."
He said linking to sterling would not backfire on Ireland but would in fact save the country a lot of the very damaging volatility which it will undoubtedly experience in the run-up to EMU.
"The next 18 months will undoubtedly be quite nightmarish for the Irish authorities in terms of exchange rate management if we persist in our determination to join EMU round one."
PRO-EMU LOBBY USES INVESTMENT ARGUMENT

The pro-EMU lobby, which includes past and present government figures, argues that it would continue to encourage direct inward investment into Ireland while the country is seen as part of the EU bloc.
This lobby contends that much of the reason for an unprecedented surge of foreign investment is that Ireland is seen as a gateway to the new single-currency Europe.

Power said this was nonsense and asked why Britain, which is not joining EMU at the moment, is still the most successful EU country in attracting foreign investment, particularly from Germany, one of EMU's driving forces.

Sweden and Britain are content to sit back and see if EMU is working. So chances are that if EMU works, Britain will eventually join in the early years of the next decade and Ireland could then comfortably follow, said Power.

"The corollary of that is that if the UK decided not to join EMU in the next decade it will be because it is not seen to be working and if it is not working Ireland would not want to be in in the first place."
